Investors paying $100 for Salesforce (CRM) stock today receive a business that produced about $8.30 of free cash flow over the last twelve months, compared with $4.20 for the median S&P 500 company. A valuation that low relative to cash generation usually points to one of two scenarios: a business on sale, or a business the market expects to shrink. So is Salesforce on sale, or shrinking?

A shrinking business would not register growth in both sales and cash, and Salesforce continues to expand on both fronts. Revenue increased 11.2% over the twelve months to July 31, 2026, while free cash flow rose to $15.2 billion from $12.5 billion a year earlier.

Shareholders hold a claim on the free cash Salesforce produces, just as they do on its profits, regardless of where the company allocates the money. Investors generally pay more for this cash generation once they notice it, and they pay more still when that cash keeps growing.

Salesforce sells software ranging from Agentforce Service to Slack. Over the twelve months to July, the company retained 77.3% of its revenue after covering the direct costs of delivering those products. The operating margin reached 21.5%, up from 19.1% two years earlier.

Running the business also requires little capital. Over those twelve months, Salesforce put 3.8% of its cash from operations into capital spending, leaving nearly all of the money as free cash flow. It has stayed above zero in every twelve-month period since July 2023, and it has roughly doubled from the $7.56 billion recorded in the twelve months to July 2023.

The company does carry significantly more debt today. Total debt stood at $41.7 billion on July 31, 2026, compared with $11.2 billion a year earlier. Over those same twelve months, Salesforce spent $35.1 billion buying back its own shares. Net of cash, that debt equals 16.6% of the company’s market value, and a portion of the cash must service these obligations before benefiting the owners. Measured against the entire business, debt included, the cash yield falls to 7.1%.

Should Tyler Technologies Stock Holders Look At Salesforce Instead?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Tyler Technologies (TYL) and Salesforce (CRM) attract investors on a single premise: customers will deploy their AI within the software they already run. Tyler sells to governments and is shifting those clients off their own servers into its own cloud infrastructure. Salesforce targets corporate buyers and is pushing them toward pricier editions featuring Agentforce agents. For Tyler shareholders, this cloud transition must drive total sales higher while the company expands its margin on little debt. Is Tyler’s cloud move paying off yet?

That payoff has not yet appeared in Tyler’s total sales. Management said cloud subscription revenue grew 21.2% in fiscal Q3 2026, the quarter ending in September. Total revenue rose 8.7% during that same period, trailing the 9.7% growth recorded a year earlier.

Tyler trimmed its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance on October 28 to a midpoint of $2,550 million, down from $2,555 million. Management attributed this reduction to deal timing. Because new deals were signed later in the year, Tyler will recognize less of their revenue in 2026. Management also said the company is well placed for faster moves to the cloud beginning in 2027.

Salesforce moved its latest guidance in the opposite direction. The company raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance on August 26 to a midpoint of $46.3 billion, up from $46.1 billion. Management said the raise includes $200 million expected from Contentful and Fin, two acquisitions the company expected to close within weeks. Before currency moves took $100 million off, management put the raise at about $300 million. These two guidance changes carry different details: Tyler made a small cut based on deal timing, and Salesforce issued a raise that, before currency moves, came partly from acquisitions.

Tyler’s operating margin over twelve months has risen each year, climbing from 13.3% in the period to September 2024 to 15.6% in the period to September 2026. Salesforce’s margin was wider still, at 21.5% in the twelve months to July 2026, a metric that has also risen each year.
Tyler has directed capital toward share buybacks and its acquisition of CODY Systems.

Is There A Risk Hiding In Salesforce Stock’s Record Quarter?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Salesforce (CRM) called its fiscal Q2 2027 a record second quarter. When that period ended on July 31, 2026, the company owed $41.7 billion in total debt, a sum close to the $43.9 billion of revenue it brought in over the past twelve months. Any cash used to pay down that debt is cash that cannot go to shareholders. So how much more does Salesforce owe than it did a year ago?

Salesforce owed $11.2 billion at the end of July 2025, meaning it accumulated most of its July 2026 debt load in a single year. That pace breaks from the company’s past. Over the five years leading up to July 2025, debt balances at the end of each July stayed between $11.2 billion and $15.5 billion.

Two other items changed over those same twelve months. Salesforce spent $35.1 billion buying back its own shares, up from $6.22 billion the year before, and management said on the August 26, 2026, call that its $25 billion accelerated share repurchase continues. At the same time, its cash and short-term investments fell to $11.4 billion, dropping from $15.4 billion a year earlier.

Salesforce would need about two years of free cash flow to clear its debt after cash. The company owed $30.3 billion more than it held in cash and short-term investments, compared with $15.2 billion of free cash flow generated over the past twelve months.

Salesforce also has fewer shares to absorb that debt. Diluted shares fell to 821 million, down from 962 million a year earlier, and management expects to repurchase at least 14% of shares outstanding through the accelerated program, which by the August call had been buying shares at an average price of $176. Each remaining share now holds a larger slice of both the profit and the debt.
Measured against the company’s market value, the debt load is modest, though above the market’s. Salesforce’s debt equals 22.9% of its market value, compared with 19.2% for the S&P 500.

When it comes to choosing which of these AI-forward software-as-a-service (SaaS) stocks deserves your money right now, a clear winner stands out.

It wasn't long ago that ServiceNow was selling off almost every day as AI companies began showing how capable AI agents can be. ServiceNow's core business is workflow automation, software that makes repetitive tasks within companies, such as submitting an IT support ticket, easier and quicker. But those types of tasks are exactly what AI agents can do really well.

ServiceNow quickly realized this and pivoted to building its business around AI. In a nutshell, ServiceNow wants to help customers deploy and manage AI agents. It can function like a control tower at an airport, directing which plane goes where and when. AI agents can operate without human intervention, so there needs to be some form of supervision, and ServiceNow's software already sits in its customers' critical IT areas.

Is The Market Ignoring The Real Growth Story In Salesforce Stock?
sum: It’s no secret that Salesforce (CRM) stock has been a tough holding. With shares down 41% over the last year, the market’s verdict seems clear: the era of hyper-growth is over, and with it, the premium valuation. The conversation is almost entirely about the top line.

But what if the most important number at Salesforce today isn’t its revenue growth? Buried in the financials is a figure that reframes the entire investment case. Over the past three years, the company’s revenue grew at a compound annual rate of 10.0%. During that same period, its GAAP earnings per share compounded at 183.7% a year. Even its adjusted earnings compounded at over 3x the top-line growth.

That is not a typo. The bottom line is growing exponentially faster than the top line. Far from being a mere accounting curiosity, this is the signature of a business that has found a different way to create value.

This gap is the result of two factors. First, Salesforce is becoming more profitable. The company’s operating margin has climbed from 9.2% three years ago, to 18.4% two years ago, to 20.5% a year ago.

Second, the company is systematically reducing its share count. By buying back stock, Salesforce has lowered its number of shares outstanding by about 11.4% over the past three years. This means the company’s profit is being divided among fewer owners, amplifying the return for each remaining share.

This brings us to the central anxiety plaguing the stock: slowing growth. Skeptics are right that 10.0% revenue growth isn’t the pace of the past. But the growth in earnings per share means the company may not need high sales growth to increase that metric. The business is generating this growth from margin expansion and buybacks.

The current valuation appears to give little credit for this shift. The stock trades at a price-to-sales multiple of 3.2, a figure that is actually below its historical average. This suggests a market fixated on the top line has overlooked the earnings growth happening underneath.

Salesforce's Agentforce platform is supposed to help companies via AI agents to handle marketing, operations, and sales, and thus far, it seems to be working. However, there's a real fear of cannibalization happening. The same AI agents helping enterprise clients could replace the seat-based subscriptions that Salesforce relies on.
